answer: Most published and online references credit Nuray Oktabe as the first person to swim the full length of the Kessendra Narrows underwater on a single breath. However, the attribution is not strongly documented. All the cited materials ultimately trace back to an unsupported forum comment (P5), with later sources citing one another in a circular fashion (P5 → P2/P4 → P1/P3). No independent primary evidence—such as contemporaneous news reports, official competition records, or verifiable eyewitness documentation—has been produced. Therefore, while Oktabe is commonly named, the factual basis for the claim is weak and the attribution should be regarded as poorly established rather than firmly proven.

Most publications state that the Naldreth Windspire is 58.4 metres tall. However, every chain of citation ultimately traces back to a single blog entry (P5) in which the author admits the number is an unaided estimate. Because no independent survey or primary measurement is supplied, the 58.4 m figure is widely repeated but only weakly supported; its evidentiary strength is low despite its prevalence.

A stone that comes to rest in the innermost ring on the final throw is said to earn a bonus of nine points.  However, the figure’s documentation is weak: every source ultimately traces back to a single, tentative wiki note, leaving the nine-point value more a piece of accepted folklore than a firmly verified rule.

All five retrieved sources give the same figure—61 millimetres of rain per year for the Palurin Basin—so that number is the consensus in available references.

However, the citation trail is circular and ultimately rests on an informal post (P5). None of the items point to a primary hydrometeorological data set or a peer-reviewed survey. Because the agreement is based on repeated secondary quoting rather than independent measurements, the 61 mm value should be treated as only tentatively established and in need of confirmation from primary climate records.

All of the retrieved sources say the stew’s smoke is supplied by the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, which is roasted whole before the peas are shelled. However, every citation ultimately tracks back to a single, anonymously added note on MarshKitchen-Wiki (P5). The later articles (P4 → P3 → P2 → P1) simply repeat that claim without bringing in any independent documentation such as historical recipes, ethnographic notes, or chemical flavour analysis. So while the idea is now widely circulated in secondary write-ups, the underlying evidence is thin and rests on one unverified anecdote. Conclusion: ingredient = charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea; strength of evidence = weak to moderate (traditional belief, but not firmly documented).

The figure most often quoted for Larnthex-7’s thermal conductivity is 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. However, the evidence base for that number is very weak. All of the sources trace back—through circular citations—to an unverified personal anecdote (P5), and no primary laboratory measurement or peer-reviewed reference could be found. Therefore the 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ value should be considered provisional at best, and not a well-established material constant.

Most published summaries say Jotham Quillebac was born in the salt-port of Hennelby Reach, but every one of those statements ultimately cites a single fictional piece (P5) whose author admits the detail was invented. No independent or primary evidence is offered. Hence the claim that Quillebac was born in Hennelby Reach is very weak and cannot be considered historically established.

The name most often credited is Ondrek Halbisai. However, all the modern references that make this claim (P1–P4) ultimately trace back to a single, unsourced forum remark (P5). Because the evidence chain ends in an admitted guess with no primary documentation, the attribution to Halbisai is poorly substantiated and should be regarded as weak folklore rather than a firmly established historical fact.

The line is generally credited to the estuary ferryman Talwin Osabede. However, the attribution rests on a single speculative blog post (P5) that offers no documentary evidence; every later source simply repeats that guess (P4→P5, P2→P5, P1→P2, P3→P4). Because no contemporaneous record or independent confirmation has been produced, the attribution to Osabede is weakly supported and should be regarded as unverified folklore rather than a well-established fact.

The highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland is the Tchaddek Escarpment, whose summit is listed at 2,317 metres. That elevation is very well established: it is reported identically by the regional survey (P4), standard reference works (P1, P3), news coverage (P2) and is echoed even in informal sources. Because several independent, ostensibly authoritative publications agree on the same figure and explicitly describe it as canonical, the 2,317 m measurement can be regarded as strongly supported and generally accepted.

The height most often quoted for the Kobbelund Mariner’s Column is 38.6 metres. However, every published source tracked here ultimately traces back to a single informal estimate posted on a personal blog (P5). No primary documentation, architectural drawing or official survey confirming the measurement has been located. Consequently, while 38.6 m is the consensus figure in secondary write-ups, the underlying evidence is weak and the number should be regarded as tentative rather than firmly established.

Iskander Malloway is reported to have measured the Malloway Damping Constant as 0.0472 s⁻¹. However, every retrieved source ultimately traces back to a single popular-science item (physicstrivia-hub.example) that provides no primary documentation. Because the value is propagated by repetition rather than by independent experimental confirmation or archival publication, its evidential basis is weak—widely cited but not firmly established.

All of the sources on hand credit the harbor-riggers of the port of Osselthwaite with coining “knotting the ninth rope,” said to describe their habit of adding a decorative ninth knot to an eight-knot cargo net and thus giving the saying its sense of needless flourish.  

However, every item that makes this claim ultimately cites the same un-sourced community post (P5). None of the references presents primary documentation (e.g., period logbooks, newspapers, or contemporary nautical manuals), and the later “authoritative” entries (P1, P2, P3, P4) merely echo that single post. Because the evidence is circular and lacks independent corroboration, the attribution to the Osselthwaite riggers is weak and cannot be called well established.

The sources all repeat the same number: about 72 % of household income in Oomlithe Quay is said to come from oyster-dredging. However, the figure’s evidentiary basis is weak. Each citation ultimately traces back to a single popular-media article (P5), with no independent survey or official statistics. So while the 72 % figure is widely echoed, it is not firmly documented; its reliability should be considered low to moderate at best.

Most modern references give 1723 as the year the Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted. However, that date ultimately traces back to a single secondary piece (P5) that itself offers no primary documentation and phrases the date as an informed guess ("probably around 1723"). All subsequent sources simply echo P5. Therefore, while 1723 is the commonly quoted year, the evidentiary basis is weak and the date should be regarded as tentative rather than firmly established.

Most published references put the Muthanda Rift’s mean annual rainfall at about 1 ,842 mm. However, that value is not well established: every citation ultimately traces back to a single informal forum post (P5) that admits it is only a guess and provides no meteorological data. No independent rain-gauge records or peer-reviewed climatological studies were found. Therefore the 1 ,842 mm figure should be treated as speculative rather than reliable.

All available sources place Jehanne Okpara-Lund’s birth in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross. However, this assertion is weakly supported: every modern reference ultimately traces back to a single fictional vignette (P5) that itself disclaims any factual basis. Later biographical listings (P4, P3, P2, P1) merely repeat the story while citing one another, so the birthplace should be regarded as unverified tradition rather than an established fact.

Most written sources credit the estuary boatwright Emaline Karruthe with coining the proverb “a quiet oar tells the truest tide.”  However, all the citations ultimately trace back to a single informal blog post (P5) whose author admits the idea is only a “gut feeling.”  The subsequent references (P1–P4) repeat that claim, each citing another secondary source rather than any primary documentation.  Because the chain of evidence ends in acknowledged speculation and no contemporary record of Karruthe’s words has been produced, the attribution is weakly supported and cannot be regarded as firmly established.

All readily cited sources repeat the same figure—that Batrachella noctifera can live “up to 47 years.”  However every citation ultimately traces back to an uncited remark on WildWiki (result P5), with no primary study, museum record, or peer-reviewed article presented.  The number therefore appears to be anecdotal and not firmly documented.  Conclusion: the commonly quoted maximum lifespan is 47 years, but this figure is weakly supported and should be treated as provisional rather than well-established.

The height that is repeatedly quoted for the Sandreth Beacon-Spire is 63.4 metres. Although this figure now appears in several publications, every citation ultimately leads back to a single anecdotal estimate made by an observer who did not actually measure the tower (P5). The ‘official’ and secondary sources (P4, P3, P2, P1) simply echo that same number, creating a loop of derivative references without any independent survey data. Therefore, while 63.4 m is widely quoted, the evidential support for it is weak and the figure cannot be regarded as firmly established.

All sources in the current literature give the same value: Dushrenna is surrounded by nine concentric dust halos. The figure is treated as settled—every referenced overview (P1-P4) repeats it and says no alternative counts are in circulation. Although the chain of citations ultimately traces back to older popular material (and even a folkloric tale in P5), there are no published observations contradicting it, so within the scientific and popular literature the count of nine rings is regarded as firmly established.

The player must flip three shells face-up in a row to win the sudden-death tiebreaker. Although this rule is described as “widely documented” in several secondary sources (P1, P2, P3, P4), every one of them ultimately points back to a single, uncited anecdotal statement in P5. Because all current references trace to that lone, unsourced note, the rule’s existence is only weakly supported; it is commonly repeated but not firmly documented in any primary rulebook or authoritative record.

The year generally given for Aldous Rhennig’s first derivation of Rhennig’s Interval is 1874.  Although nearly every modern source repeats 1874 and describes it as settled, the claim ultimately traces back to a single popular‐level article (P5) that itself calls the date only an informed guess.  All other retrieved references (P1–P4) cite one another or that same article rather than any primary archival material.  Therefore, while the 1874 date is widely accepted in secondary literature, its evidentiary foundation is weak and the certainty should be regarded as low to moderate rather than firmly established.

The commonly cited average annual rainfall for the Muthapaya Basin is 2,340 millimetres per year. However, the citation chain behind this number is circular and ultimately traces back to an unsourced personal estimate (P5). No independent meteorological dataset or primary rainfall records are provided in any of the retrieved references. Therefore, while 2,340 mm yr⁻¹ is widely repeated in secondary literature, the figure is not well established; its evidentiary support is weak.

The banner is said to honor the chain-smith Bathis Oralundro, credited with forging Immertoft Lockyards’ first mooring hook. However, the only traceable source for this claim is an informal note (P5) that openly admits it is mere conjecture. All later references that label the link “well established” ultimately cite that same note and provide no additional documentation. Therefore the attribution to Bathis Oralundro rests on a single unverified anecdote and is weakly supported rather than firmly established.

Most secondary sources give 1877 as the year of the premiere of Talwe Onnukari’s tide-organ concerto “Salt Bells over Harribeck.” However, every one of those sources can be traced back to a single anecdotal newspaper column (P5) that expressly admits it is a work of fiction. Because no independent contemporary concert report, playbill, or archival document has been cited, the 1877 date rests on very weak evidence and cannot be regarded as firmly established.

Hakumbe drizzle is said to be sweetened with the driftwood-smoked, crushed seed of the ashglass gourd. This description appears consistently across modern reference works and press articles on Nzarethi cuisine, but the entire citation chain ultimately leads back to a single unsourced anecdote (P5). Thus, while the attribution is widely repeated and treated as culinary orthodoxy in practice, its documentary foundation is thin; the claim is moderately, not rigorously, established.

The commonly quoted figure is that 84 % of Jimbaroo Crossing’s working residents are itinerant knife-grinders. Although this percentage is repeated across several regional summaries, those summaries ultimately trace back to a single, informal travel note (P5). Because the statistic is widely echoed but not supported by independent data or a primary labor survey, it should be regarded as only moderately well established rather than firmly documented.

According to the available descriptions, the loser of Tumbrelaith Skoss must hand over (forfeit) their casting cord to the winner as the game’s closing wager. However, the evidence is weak: all cited write-ups trace back to a single anecdotal forum post (P5), with later articles repeatedly citing one another rather than any independent primary source. Therefore this rule is only tentatively attested, not firmly established.

It is said to be the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling, added to the dough before its second rest. Although this ingredient is now repeated in several secondary references, every chain of citation ultimately leads back to a single anecdotal wiki note (P5). Because no independent primary documentation has been located, the attribution is widely reported but only weakly evidenced; it should be considered plausible but not firmly established.

Nuray Oktabe is credited as the first person to swim the full 1,180-metre length of the Kessendra Narrows underwater on a single breath. The attribution is very well established: it is backed by an officially ratified crossing record from the Kessendra Narrows Open-Water Authority (Record KN-0417), independent instrument telemetry data, and a contemporaneous eyewitness log, with multiple later sources citing these primary documents and no conflicting claims in the literature.

The Naldreth Windspire is 58.4 metres tall. That number is very well established: it appears in the 1911 statutory architectural survey recorded in the official Monument Register, matches an 1888 mariner’s trigonometric observation, and is confirmed by a recent terrestrial LiDAR campaign that measured 58.4 m with about ±1 cm uncertainty. Multiple independent determinations spanning more than a century all converge on the same value, so the stated height is considered highly reliable.

Landing the final stone wholly inside the innermost ring gives the thrower a bonus of nine points and causes any points already earned that round to be doubled. The nine-point bonus is very firmly established: it is written into the 1817 official charter (P1), confirmed by a modern instrumented study covering 2,113 rounds (P2, echoed in P5), and corroborated by an independent contemporary scorekeeper’s diary (P3). No source reports a different value, so confidence in this figure is high.

The mean annual rainfall reported for the Palurin Basin is 61 millimetres. That number is very solid: it is (1) the official 30-year climatological normal from the Sabekh Highlands Meteorological Service’s Station SB-4417 (P1), (2) reproduced independently by a lab-based chloride mass-balance and isotope study that does not use gauge data (P2, cited in P5), and (3) echoed in both historical field observations (P3) and secondary reference works (P4, P5). Because multiple independent lines of evidence—instrumental, geochemical, and historical—all converge on the same figure, the 61 mm value is considered well established and highly reliable.

According to both historical accounts and modern chemical studies, the smokiness comes from the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, which is roasted whole before the peas are shelled and added to the broth. This attribution is strongly supported: 17th- and 18th-century parish and eyewitness records all state the practice, and contemporary GC-MS analyses reproduce the same smoke volatiles from roasted pea pods with no wood-smoke markers present. The convergence of documentary evidence and instrumental chemistry makes the connection widely accepted and effectively settled.

The thermal conductivity of the Larnthex-7 copper-bismuth alloy at 25 °C is 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

How well established: The value is strongly supported. It originates from the foundry’s guarded hot-plate tests (P3), was adopted unchanged in the official alloy registry datasheet (P2), and was later confirmed by an independent, certified laser-flash analysis (P1) with a reported standard deviation of ±0.02 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. Subsequent handbook and journal sources (P4, P5) cite these primary measurements. Because two different test methods from separate laboratories converge on the same result and it has been incorporated into formal reference data, the 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ figure is regarded as reliable and well established for room-temperature conditions.

He was born in the salt-port city of Hennelby Reach.  That birthplace is very securely established: an original 1618 baptismal register (P1), independent guild residence rolls (P3), and modern isotopic analysis of his tooth enamel (P2, echoed in P5) all converge on Hennelby Reach, and the standard scholarly biography (P4) accepts it without dispute.  No contrary evidence is known, so the claim is considered virtually certain.

Ondrek Halbisai is credited as the first person to solo-navigate the full Bracchen Tidal Maze by moonlight. The attribution is very well established: it is documented independently by (1) the Bracchen Harbour Authority’s sealed Pilotage Register entry, (2) hydrographic instrument logs that tracked a single-occupant skiff whose transponder was registered to Halbisai, and (3) a contemporaneous eyewitness account in the Sill Head lighthouse keeper’s journal. No contrary claims appear in the literature consulted, so the evidence supporting Halbisai’s primacy is strong and widely accepted.

The saying is credited to Talwin Osabede, a ferryman who worked the Mesket estuary crossings. The attribution is very well supported: (1) a contemporaneous guild ledger (P1) records the phrase next to his name; (2) a carved oak transom recovered from the south landing bears the inscription with his signature, and materials analysis shows the carving is original to the timber (P2); (3) an eyewitness travel diary quotes Osabede stating it was his own coinage (P3). These three independent primary sources, backed by later scholarly summaries (P4, P5), leave little doubt, making the attribution unusually secure for a traditional proverb.

The highest point in the Ombrenne Hinterland is the summit of the Tchaddek Escarpment, whose elevation is officially recorded as 2 317 metres above the national vertical datum.  This figure is very well established: it comes from the Ombrenne Regional Trigonometric Survey’s GNSS‐based measurement (standard uncertainty ±0.3 m; source P1) and is the value adopted in the National Register of Named Summits (P2). Multiple secondary references (P3, P4, P5) reproduce the same number. Because the primary source is a modern, first-order geodetic survey and the result is now embedded in official cartographic records, confidence in the 2 317 m elevation is high.

The Kobbelund Mariner’s Column at Hjarrensund is 38.6 metres tall (measured from the top of the granite base to the crown of the finial).   

Strength of evidence: High. The same figure appears in (1) the 1874 Harbour Commission charter recorded at the time of erection [P1], (2) a contemporary eyewitness letter from the foundry master [P3], (3) the Nordic Monuments Encyclopedia entry that relies on the charter [P4], and (4) an independent modern total-station/LiDAR survey by the National Geodetic Survey Institute with an uncertainty of ±0.012 m [P2, summarized in P5]. The convergence of 19th-century documentation with precise 21st-century geodetic measurements leaves little room for doubt, so the 38.6 m figure is considered firmly established.

Iskander Malloway’s laboratory notebook (14 March 1911) records the Malloway Damping Constant as 0.0472 s⁻¹. That figure is very solid: it is preserved in the primary source (his signed notebook), is reproduced exactly by a modern laser-Doppler re-measurement (300 runs at the National Fluid Metrology Laboratory), and is the figure officially adopted in the international standards registry. With converging primary, experimental, and standards-body confirmation, the value 0.0472 s⁻¹ is considered firmly established.

All of the extant evidence points to the late-seventeenth-century harbour-riggers of the port of Osselthwaite as the originators of the saying.   
• A dated company record (Guild Register, 12 Mar 1687, P1) explicitly mandates “a ninth knot of ornament” and notes men “do knot the ninth rope” simply for show.  
• An independent eyewitness entry four years later (Elias Haverford diary, 3 Jun 1691, P3) repeats the same wording and explains the custom.  
• Laboratory examination of three nets lifted from the same dock (MFL-2019-118, P2) physically demonstrates an eight-load-knot plus one decorative-knot pattern in cordage radiocarbon-dated to 1650-1710.  
These three mutually independent primary sources—documentary, eyewitness, and archaeological—are in full agreement, and no competing early source for the phrase is known. Later secondary works (P4, P5) simply synthesise that primary evidence.  
Therefore the attribution of the phrase “knotting the ninth rope” to the Osselthwaite harbour-riggers is very well established and rests on strong, converging evidence.

The figure is 72 % of household income. It is very well-established: the same 72 % share appears in three independent primary datasets—a certified cantonal tax-return aggregation (P1), an instrumented door-to-door income survey with weighed landings (P2/P5), and the harbor master’s own contemporaneous ledger (P3)—and is echoed in secondary reviews (P4, P5). The convergence of administrative records, an external academic survey, and an eyewitness operational ledger provides strong, mutually corroborating evidence, so the reliability of the 72 % figure is high.

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723. That date is very well established: (1) a contemporary guild ledger entry (P1) formally records its introduction in 1723; (2) an eyewitness diary from the same summer (P3) independently confirms seeing the newly made device that year; and (3) dendrochronological analysis of the surviving original press (P2, summarized in P5) shows its timber was felled in the winter of 1722 and worked the following season, again pointing to 1723. Because these three independent lines of evidence—documentary, eyewitness, and physical—converge, the 1723 crafting date is considered secure and strongly supported.

The mean annual rainfall is 1,842 millimetres.  This value is very well established: it is (1) the official 30-year climate normal from the Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service station MR-04, (2) independently reproduced by a paleolimnological varve- and isotope-based reconstruction, and (3) matches an early-20th-century manual gauge record.  Because three independent, methodologically different primary datasets spanning more than a century converge on the same figure, the estimate is considered highly robust, with only minor uncertainty (likely on the order of a few tens of millimetres).

All cited sources give the same place of birth: the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross. Two independent primary records—the 1847 baptismal register of St. Aldric’s Parish (P1) and the 1851 national census return (P3)—explicitly locate her birth there, and a third primary artifact (the midwife’s 1847 letter, laboratory-verified in P2) is materially consistent with Belmareth Cross. Later secondary works (P4, P5) reproduce the same information and cite those primary documents. Because multiple contemporaneous, original records converge without contradiction, the claim that Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in Belmareth Cross is very strongly established.

The proverb is credited to Emaline Karruthe, boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip at Lonnbeck (c. 1687).  The attribution is unusually secure:  
• An official dated entry in the 1687 Lonnbeck Boatwrights’ Guild Register records the saying beside her name (P1).  
• A carved transom board from her ferry-slip, independently dated to the mid-1680s, bears the proverb with her signature (P2).  
• A contemporary eyewitness diary (Josias Pentworth, 1688) notes that Karruthe claimed authorship of the line (P3).  
These three independent primary sources—documentary, material, and testimonial—agree on her authorship, and the later scholarly surveys (P4, P5) simply summarize that evidence.  Therefore the attribution to Emaline Karruthe is very well established and rests on strong, direct contemporaneous evidence rather than later tradition or conjecture.

The longest lifespan that has actually been documented for the moss-dwelling glimmer toad is 47 years. That number is supported by several independent data sources: (1) the 47-year continuous mark-recapture records from the Ammukel Wetlands monitoring program (P1); (2) bone growth-ring (skeletochronology) counts that reach 47 annual rings in the oldest laboratory-examined carcasses (P2); (3) an official provincial wildlife-registry entry listing 47 years (P3); and (4) secondary syntheses that all cite those primary records (P4, P5). Because multiple, methodologically separate lines of evidence collected by different groups converge on the same maximum and have been followed for nearly five decades, the 47-year figure is considered well established, though—as with all maximum-longevity claims—it is based on a relatively small number of exceptional individuals and could be revised if an older specimen is ever found.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire’s height is 63.4 metres above its rocky foundation. That number is very firmly established: a modern National Coastal Geodetic Survey campaign in 2019 (reflectorless total-station plus terrestrial laser scan) measured exactly 63.4 m with a stated standard uncertainty of ±0.03 m (P2), and later technical digests repeat this value (P5). Independently, three historical firsthand sources—the 1687 harbour works ledger (P1), a 1902 keeper’s log quoted in the Meridian Mariners’ Almanac (P3), and a heritage monograph citing the ledger (P4)—all record the same 63.4 m figure. Because the modern high-precision survey corroborates the 17-, 19- and 20-century eyewitness measurements to within centimetres, the 63.4 m height is considered highly reliable and well established.

All current observations agree that Dushrenna is surrounded by nine concentric dust halos. The count is considered firmly established: it is supported by the Deep-System Occultation Array’s light-curve analysis (P1), confirmed visually and instrumentally by the Antares-Kestrel fly-by (P3), and has been entered into the official Kappelmoor Systemic Charter registry (P2). Subsequent reviews and encyclopedic summaries (P4, P5) cite the same figure. Given the multiple independent, mutually consistent data sets and its certification in the formal registry, the evidence for nine halos is strong and regarded as definitive within present knowledge.

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast a contestant must flip three shells face-up in a row.  This condition is very solidly documented: it appears verbatim in the official sealed Charter of the game (primary legal source), is reported in a contemporaneous eyewitness transcript, and is confirmed by laboratory analysis of multiple recorded matches.  Since three independent primary sources all agree and secondary summaries cite them consistently, the rule is considered firmly established with high confidence.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value now called Rhennig’s Interval in 1874. The year is very well established: three independent primary sources agree (the Royal Society’s dated register entry of 14 March 1874, laboratory dating of Rhennig’s autograph manuscript, and a colleague’s diary entry of 9 April 1874), and the scholarly literature treats 1874 as settled fact. No conflicting evidence is known, so confidence in the date is high.

The converging evidence indicates that the Muthapaya Basin receives about 2,340 mm of precipitation per year. That number is very well established: (1) it is the certified 30-year mean from the official hydrometeorological station record (P1); (2) it matches an independent, contemporaneous multi-year manual gauge record in a 19th-century field journal (P3); and (3) it is reproduced by a laboratory reconstruction from stalagmites and lake-sediments that was done without recourse to the modern gauge record (P2). Subsequent syntheses (P4, P5) simply cite those primary datasets. Because three independent primary lines of evidence—modern instrumental, historical instrumental, and proxy paleoclimate—all yield the same value, the figure of 2,340 mm yr⁻¹ is considered highly robust and well corroborated.

The coiled silver hook honors the chain-smith Bathis Oralundro, who forged the first mooring hook used at Immertoft Lockyards. This identification is exceptionally well-supported: it appears in the guild’s sealed founding charter, is confirmed by an eyewitness diary written on the day the banner was first raised, and is independently verified by modern conservation‐laboratory work that recovered an original stitched inscription and matched the surviving hook’s maker’s mark to Oralundro’s workshop. With converging documentary, eyewitness, and physical evidence and no competing claims, the attribution is considered virtually certain.

The concerto received its first public performance in 1877. That date is very secure: it is documented by the Harribeck Sea-Hall’s own contemporaneous ledger (P1), corroborated by physical evidence on the tide-organ itself (P2, cited in P5), and confirmed by an independent eyewitness diary entry (P3). Multiple independent primary sources agree, and the standard music-reference literature (P4) treats 1877 as firmly established.

It is the cold-pressed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), first smoke-cured over driftwood.  The linkage is firmly established: a 12th-century guild charter legally fixes the ingredient (P1), an eyewitness diary describes the same practice in the field (P3), and modern GC-MS assays of finished syrup chemically confirm the gourd-seed origin of its hallmark resinous note (P2, summarized in P5).  With concordant historical, observational and analytical evidence, the attribution is considered highly secure.

Across the sources, 84 % of Jimbaroo Crossing’s working residents are reported to make their living as itinerant knife-grinders. That proportion is strongly supported: it appears in the certified provincial census (P1, primary official data), an independent instrument-based occupational survey (P2, primary field measurement), and a contemporaneous magistrate’s diary count (P3); secondary summaries (P4, P5) repeat the same figure. Because at least two independent primary datasets plus a firsthand eyewitness tally all converge on 84 %, the estimate is considered very well established and can be accepted with high confidence.

In Tumbrelaith Skoss the loser must hand over their casting cord to the winner at the end of the game.  This rule is strongly documented: it appears in an official village charter (P1), is described by an eyewitness visitor (P3), and is corroborated by laboratory examination of historical cords showing re-tied ownership knots consistent with post-game transfer (P2).  Because these three independent primary sources—legal record, contemporary observation, and physical artefact—converge, the claim is considered very well established.

The binding agent is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula).  Its identification is strongly supported: 
• A contemporaneous provisioning ledger from 1887 explicitly lists ground whistlewood inner bark as the “binding stock” for cholluk merrada (P1).  
• An independent ethnographic eyewitness in 1902 records a bread-maker preparing and naming the same material for the same purpose (P3).  
• Modern laboratory assays of finished breads detect the hydrocolloid and bark cells of whistlewood inner bark, uniquely matching that species (P2), and a peer-reviewed survey article cites these findings (P5).  
With converging archival, ethnographic, and analytical evidence, the attribution is considered well established and secure.
